proposals.name: Decisive Fit to Explicit Ask
proposals.rationale: Deliberate awards favor answers that visibly resolve the bounty’s central objective.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when it delivers a clear recommendation for the requested outcome; low when it leaves the reader to choose among tangents. It does not apply when the question lacks a discernible objective.

proposals.name: Evidence-Grounded Diagnosis
proposals.rationale: Evidence-based reasoning makes an answer easier to trust and deliberately select.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when claims are tied to observable code, errors, or constraints in the question; low when they rely on unsupported speculation. It does not apply when no diagnostic evidence is provided.

proposals.name: Runnable Minimal Demonstration
proposals.rationale: A directly runnable demonstration provides strong practical evidence of answer quality.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the included example can run as shown and isolates the relevant behavior; low when it contains missing definitions or unresolved fragments. It does not apply to purely conceptual questions.

proposals.name: Verification Transparency
proposals.rationale: Transparent verification helps a bounty-setter distinguish demonstrated solutions from plausible speculation.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer reports testing, expected output, or a reproducible validation method; low when unverified code is presented with certainty. It does not apply when verification cannot reasonably be performed.

proposals.name: Assumption Disclosure
proposals.rationale: Explicit assumptions reduce ambiguity during deliberate evaluation and implementation.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when required inputs, environments, versions, or preconditions are explicit; low when hidden assumptions could materially change the result. It does not apply to assumption-free answers.

proposals.name: Version Alignment
proposals.rationale: Version fit strongly affects whether a technically sound answer is actually award-worthy.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when version-sensitive advice matches the question’s stated context and flags relevant incompatibilities; low when it silently depends on a different era or release. It does not apply when versions are irrelevant or unspecified.

proposals.name: Dependency Proportionality
proposals.rationale: Practical bounty decisions weigh solution benefit against new operational and maintenance burden.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when added packages, services, or configuration are minimal or justified; low when unnecessary machinery increases adoption cost. It does not apply when no dependencies are introduced.

proposals.name: Operational Safety Tradeoff
proposals.rationale: Responsible handling of consequences distinguishes deliberately awardable solutions from merely functional ones.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when security, privacy, data-loss, or resource risks are identified and responsibly handled; low when a risky shortcut is offered without qualification. It does not apply when no material operational risk exists.

proposals.name: Scale-Appropriate Efficiency
proposals.rationale: A bounty answer should remain useful under the workload the asker describes.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when time, memory, I/O, or concurrency choices fit the scale stated in the question; low when obvious bottlenecks are ignored. It does not apply when scale has no practical bearing.

proposals.name: Failure-Recovery Guidance
proposals.rationale: Recovery guidance increases real-world usefulness beyond initial success.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when it explains what to inspect or change after likely failure; low when it covers only the happy path. It does not apply when the task has no meaningful failure mode.

proposals.name: Alternative Selection Logic
proposals.rationale: Deliberate awards favor judgment that helps the asker make a concrete choice.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when alternatives are compared against stated constraints and one is recommended; low when the answer supplies an unprioritized catalog. It does not apply when only one reasonable approach is presented.

proposals.name: Customization Guidance
proposals.rationale: Clear adaptation boundaries make an answer more actionable and less misleading.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when placeholders, environment-specific values, and required edits are clearly identified; low when copied code appears ready but cannot be adapted safely. It does not apply when the solution is entirely generic.

proposals.name: Claim-Code Consistency
proposals.rationale: Internal consistency is a visible signal of careful, deliberate authorship.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when prose, comments, and code describe the same behavior; low when explanations promise behavior the code does not implement. It does not apply when the answer contains no substantive code or claims.

proposals.name: Distinct Incremental Contribution
proposals.rationale: Manual bounty awards often recognize added value rather than repetition.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer adds a materially different solution, diagnosis, or insight beyond cited work; low when it merely endorses or lightly paraphrases another answer. It does not apply when no prior work is mentioned.

proposals.name: Limitation Candor
proposals.rationale: Candid boundaries help evaluators judge whether the answer merits intentional recognition.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when meaningful limitations, uncertainty, or known exceptions are acknowledged; low when broad guarantees are made without qualification. It does not apply when the method has no material limitations visible from the text.

proposals.name: Answer length
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Total prose and code length, judged by approximate word count or visible extent.

proposals.name: Code share
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Whether code occupies most of the answer relative to explanatory prose.

proposals.name: Link density
proposals.parent: answer timing, cross-posting, and reputation dynamics
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Count visible external hyperlinks or linked references per answer.

proposals.name: First-person experience
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Presence of claims such as “I found,” “worked for me,” or “my solution.”

proposals.name: Other-answer references
proposals.parent: answer order and competitive answer dynamics
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Explicit mentions of accepted, voted, linked, or previously posted answers.

proposals.name: Version markers
proposals.parent: question age and temporal technology cohort
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Presence of explicit software versions, release numbers, dates, or version-specific APIs.

proposals.name: Beginner scaffolding
proposals.parent: asker sophistication and respondent audience selection
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Use of analogies, “in simpler words,” or step-by-step teaching language.

proposals.name: Caveat boilerplate
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Generic disclaimers such as “AFAIK,” “not tested,” or “as far as I know.”

proposals.name: Markup density
proposals.parent: platform formatting norms and house style
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Frequency of code fences, blockquotes, headings, bullets, or other Markdown structure.

proposals.name: Orthographic polish
proposals.parent: time pressure and answerer reputation dynamics
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Rate of visible spelling, grammar, capitalization, or typographical errors.

proposals.name: Answer length
proposals.parent: answer order, timing, and answerer identity
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Total answer length in words and characters, including unusually long digressions.

proposals.name: Code-block density
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Proportion of the answer occupied by fenced or indented code, and the number of separate code blocks.

proposals.name: External-link density
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Number of hyperlinks and the presence of links to documentation, repositories, or other answers.

proposals.name: Version-era markers
proposals.parent: answer timing relative to the bounty
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: References to Python versions, deprecated APIs, old domains, or phrases such as “ancient question.”

proposals.name: Accepted-answer references
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Explicit mentions of accepted answers, other answers, or what solved the asker’s problem.

proposals.name: Personal success claims
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Statements such as “this worked for me,” “I implemented,” or “ended up using.”

proposals.name: Spelling-error frequency
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Count of conspicuous misspellings, typos, or grammatical errors in the prose.

proposals.name: Quote-block frequency
proposals.parent: answer timing and answerer house style
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Presence and amount of blockquoted material copied from the question, documentation, or another answer.

proposals.name: Library-name prominence
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Number of prominent mentions of recognizable frameworks, libraries, or platforms in the answer.

proposals.name: Self-promotional framing
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Mentions of the author’s fork, repository, blog, product, or personal implementation.

proposals.name: Scope Closure
proposals.rationale: Manual awards favor answers that visibly finish the requested task rather than supplying an attractive fragment.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the answer completes the path from the stated situation to the intended result, including application and interpretation; low when it supplies only an isolated fact or snippet. It does not apply to narrowly scoped fact questions.

proposals.name: Self-Contained Sufficiency
proposals.rationale: A reviewer can award a usable answer without reconstructing missing setup from links or context.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when required definitions, imports, assumptions, and steps appear in the answer; low when success depends on unexplained links or omitted context. It does not apply when the question itself supplies all necessary context.

proposals.name: Outcome Observability
proposals.rationale: Stated success conditions let a human judge determine whether the answer solved the practical need.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the answer states what successful behavior or output should look like; low when users cannot tell whether the solution worked. It does not apply to purely stylistic or definitional requests.

proposals.name: Verification Evidence
proposals.rationale: Concrete checks reduce uncertainty about whether the proposed fix works as written.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when an executable check, observed output, or targeted test supports the claim; low when the solution is merely asserted. It does not apply when no meaningful behavior can be tested.

proposals.name: Constraint Preservation
proposals.rationale: Satisfying interacting constraints demonstrates closer reading and higher practical value.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the solution satisfies all explicit environmental, security, performance, and format constraints together; low when it silently violates one. It does not apply when the question states no meaningful constraints.

proposals.name: Diagnostic Causal Chain
proposals.rationale: A causal account makes the remedy trustworthy rather than lucky trial-and-error.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the answer connects the observed symptom to a mechanism and then to a fix; low when it gives a generic or weakly connected remedy. It does not apply to straightforward how-to questions without a reported problem.

proposals.name: Assumption Disclosure
proposals.rationale: Explicit scope conditions prevent overgeneralization and support deliberate selection.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when version, platform, input, or configuration assumptions are explicit and separated from guarantees; low when hidden assumptions obscure applicability. It does not apply when such conditions cannot affect the answer.

proposals.name: Procedural Sequencing
proposals.rationale: Correct sequencing reduces implementation errors and increases immediate usability.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when instructions appear in dependency order with clear transition points; low when steps are unordered or require guesswork about what comes first. It does not apply to answers requiring no procedure.

proposals.name: Option Discrimination
proposals.rationale: Decision rules turn alternatives into actionable expertise instead of uncurated possibilities.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when alternatives include explicit conditions for choosing among them; low when they are listed without decision guidance. It does not apply when one reasonable approach clearly suffices.

proposals.name: Tradeoff Calibration
proposals.rationale: Proportionate tradeoffs reveal mature judgment without rewarding boilerplate warnings.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when material costs and risks are specific and proportionate; low when consequential downsides are omitted or generic warnings overwhelm the answer. It does not apply when alternatives have no meaningful tradeoffs.

proposals.name: Recovery Guidance
proposals.rationale: Actionable recovery paths preserve value when predictable failures occur.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when likely failure messages or next diagnostic steps are actionable; low when the user is stranded after the first attempt fails. It does not apply when failure is implausible or irrelevant.

proposals.name: Boundary-Case Targeting
proposals.rationale: Relevant edge cases reveal whether the answer was thought through beyond the happy path.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when examples or tests probe edge cases relevant to the proposed method; low when only the happy path supports broad claims. It does not apply when the task has no plausible boundary cases.

proposals.name: Variant Adaptability
proposals.rationale: Adaptations extend practical usefulness while remaining anchored to the asker’s situation.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the answer shows explicit small changes for nearby variants of the supplied code or data; low when a generic snippet requires guesswork. It does not apply when no nearby variants are foreseeable.

proposals.name: Premise Correction
proposals.rationale: Constructive correction signals unusually strong understanding of the actual problem.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the answer identifies a flawed premise while still serving the underlying need; low when it blindly follows the premise or only dismisses it. It does not apply when the premise is sound.

proposals.name: Reference Independence
proposals.rationale: Self-sufficient explanations are more directly awardable than answers outsourcing value to inaccessible sources.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when reasoning and instructions remain usable without opening external links; low when citations substitute for explanation. It does not apply when the answer contains no external references.

proposals.name: SHORT SNIPPET FORMAT
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: The answer is no more than one sentence plus a code fragment or link. This may proxy early, rapid answers or answerer style rather than deliberate merit.

proposals.name: CODE-DOMINANT LAYOUT
proposals.parent: who answers this kind of question
proposals.description: >=70% code or output | DESCRIPTION: At least 70% of the visible answer consists of code, console output, or stack traces. This can reflect answerer type or house style independently of awarded merit.

proposals.name: LINK-HEAVY ANSWER
proposals.description: >=3 external links | DESCRIPTION: The answer contains three or more external hyperlinks, especially documentation, repository, or user-profile links. Link habits may identify established answerers or reusable responses.

proposals.name: GENERIC BOILERPLATE
proposals.description: Contains stock disclaimer | DESCRIPTION: The answer includes phrases such as “not tested,” “hope this helps,” “for completeness,” or “worked for me” without adding technical content. Such reusable wording can proxy answerer identity or cross-posting.

proposals.name: OTHER-ANSWER REFERENCE
proposals.description: Mentions another answer | DESCRIPTION: The answer explicitly refers to an accepted, current, highly voted, or linked answer. This can mark late arrival or answer-order effects rather than the answer’s standalone merit.

proposals.name: BOUNTY-AWARE WORDING
proposals.description: Mentions bounty or award | DESCRIPTION: The answer explicitly mentions the bounty, awarding, duplicate status, or the asker’s need to choose an answer. This may reveal bounty timing or heightened attention.

proposals.name: VERSION-ERA MARKERS
proposals.description: Uses dated ecosystem syntax | DESCRIPTION: The answer uses clearly era-specific syntax, APIs, URLs, or version labels, such as Python-2 print statements or obsolete documentation domains. This can proxy posting time and compatibility cohort.

proposals.name: TOPIC-SPECIFIC JARGON
proposals.parent: who answers this kind of question
proposals.description: Dense package vocabulary | DESCRIPTION: The answer contains unusually concentrated terminology from one named framework or package, with little general explanation. Topic popularity and specialist answer pools may influence awards independently of merit.

proposals.name: SELF-PROMOTIONAL MARKERS
proposals.description: Links own implementation | DESCRIPTION: The answer identifies an “implemented,” “forked,” or personal repository, or repeatedly uses first-person ownership language. This may proxy reputation, visibility, or answerer networks.

proposals.name: MARKUP-HEAVY PRESENTATION
proposals.description: Many headings and blocks | DESCRIPTION: The answer uses at least three headings, block quotes, or separately fenced code blocks. Consistent formatting may be a house-style or answerer-identity marker unrelated to the underlying solution.

proposals.name: Firsthand Resolution Evidence
proposals.rationale: Concrete success reports increase confidence that the answer earned deliberate reward through demonstrated resolution.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer reports a concrete observed result for the asked case; low when it remains hypothetical. Does not apply when the answer makes no executable or outcome claim.

proposals.name: Comparative Novelty
proposals.rationale: Distinct additions are more likely to attract discretionary reward than duplicative restatements.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when it adds a materially distinct solution or insight relative to alternatives explicitly mentioned; low when it merely repeats them. Does not apply when no comparison or prior approach is mentioned.

proposals.name: Specific-Constraint Fit
proposals.rationale: Solving unusual constraints signals value beyond generic correctness.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when it directly resolves a concrete, unusual constraint stated in the question; low when it gives a generic solution that leaves that constraint untouched. Does not apply when no such constraint is stated.

proposals.name: Empirical Validation Detail
proposals.rationale: Direct checks make usefulness legible and reduce reliance on trust.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when tests, outputs, reproduced errors, or other direct checks support the claim; low when executable claims are unchecked. Does not apply to purely conceptual answers.

proposals.name: Reproducibility Specificity
proposals.rationale: Specific setup information makes solutions reliably transferable.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when necessary environment, version, setup, and input assumptions are stated; low when success depends on unstated conditions. Does not apply to environment-independent explanations.

proposals.name: Tradeoff Justification
proposals.rationale: Explicit tradeoffs reveal judgment tailored to practical constraints.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when alternatives are compared using practical constraints and one choice is justified; low when options are listed without decision criteria. Does not apply when only one reasonable approach is presented.

proposals.name: Version-Horizon Awareness
proposals.rationale: Version awareness signals durable judgment and protects against brittle advice.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer distinguishes versions, deprecations, or compatibility horizons; low when version-sensitive advice is stated universally. Does not apply when the technique is version-independent.

proposals.name: Calibrated Confidence
proposals.rationale: Calibrated claims make trustworthiness easier to assess.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when tested facts, inferences, and uncertainties are clearly distinguished; low when the answer overclaims or hedges without commitment. Does not apply when the answer makes no uncertainty-relevant claims.

proposals.name: Minimal-Change Design
proposals.rationale: Lower adoption cost can make an otherwise equivalent answer preferable.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the solution preserves the user's architecture and changes only what is needed; low when it proposes an unnecessarily invasive rewrite. Does not apply to greenfield questions.

proposals.name: Resolution Closure
proposals.rationale: A clear endpoint converts technical content into an immediately usable resolution.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer ends with a clear recommendation, next action, and success condition; low when the reader must decide what to do. Does not apply to purely definitional questions.

proposals.name: Thread-Level Synthesis
proposals.rationale: Synthesis demonstrates awareness of the answer landscape and incremental value.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer situates itself among prior approaches and identifies its nonredundant contribution; low when it cites or repeats others without adding value. Does not apply when no prior approach is mentioned.

proposals.name: Corrective Accountability
proposals.rationale: Visible correction signals accountability and thoughtful resolution.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer acknowledges a prior mistake or limitation and supplies a concrete correction; low when problems are acknowledged but unresolved. Does not apply when no correction context exists.

proposals.name: Causal Diagnostic Mapping
proposals.rationale: Causal mapping makes diagnostic value easier to recognize and reward.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when symptoms or errors are explicitly linked to a cause and targeted fix; low when changes are prescribed without causal connection. Does not apply to nondiagnostic questions.

proposals.name: Integration Handoff Completeness
proposals.rationale: Complete handoff details reduce follow-up effort and increase practical usefulness.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the answer specifies where, how, and in what sequence to integrate the solution; low when implementation placement is ambiguous. Does not apply to self-contained snippets.

proposals.name: Assumption Disclosure
proposals.rationale: Transparent assumptions prevent mismatch and reveal practical judgment.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when material assumptions are stated and conditional alternatives are provided; low when the answer silently commits to one uncertain interpretation. Does not apply when the question is fully specified.

proposals.name: Long answer with extensive code
proposals.description: Answer contains substantially more prose and code than a minimal solution, regardless of whether the additional material resolves the asker's problem.

proposals.name: High markup and code density
proposals.description: Answer is dominated by fenced code, quotations, headings, or links rather than plain explanatory prose.

proposals.name: First-person anecdotal framing
proposals.parent: who answers this kind of question
proposals.description: Answer uses phrases such as “worked for me,” “I found,” or “my solution,” presenting personal experience rather than an impersonal explanation.

proposals.name: Accepted-answer or vote references
proposals.description: Answer explicitly mentions accepted answers, votes, other responders, or building on another posted answer.

proposals.name: Same-site answer linking
proposals.description: Answer prominently links to another answer on the question-and-answer site, especially as attribution or a substitute for explanation.

proposals.name: Version-era terminology
proposals.description: Answer contains conspicuous version numbers, legacy APIs, or historically dated platform terminology.

proposals.name: Question-text phrase repetition
proposals.description: Answer repeats distinctive wording, identifiers, or phrases from the question without adding corresponding clarification.

proposals.name: Informal proofreading errors
proposals.description: Answer has multiple spelling, grammar, or typographical errors, including malformed words or casual self-corrections.

proposals.name: Vendor or library name salience
proposals.description: Answer repeatedly foregrounds a particular framework, cloud vendor, package, or product name.

proposals.name: Highly hedged recommendation language
proposals.parent: asker voting behavior and answerer confidence
proposals.description: Answer relies on phrases such as “I think,” “might,” “as far as I know,” or “try this” instead of clearly stated claims.

proposals.name: Answer targets the asker's specific artifact
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer quotes, names, or reproduces something unique to the asker's own post (their variable names, their traceback text, their DataFrame, their config file) and modifies it; scores low when the code is a self-contained generic demo that would read identically under any similar question. Not applicable to conceptual questions with no user code.

proposals.name: Diagnoses cause before giving fix
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer states why the failure or behavior occurs (naming the mechanism, the missed step, the library constraint) and only then gives the remedy; scores low when it presents a code block or setting change with no causal account. Applies to all debugging/error questions.

proposals.name: Verified-run evidence versus untested proposal
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer shows actual output it obtained (REPL transcript, printed DataFrame, error text produced by running the suggestion, timing numbers); scores low when it only shows input code with no evidence anyone executed it. Does not apply to answers that are pure prose links.

proposals.name: Hedged guess language
proposals.description: Scores high (bad) when the answer opens with or is dominated by uncertainty markers about its own correctness ("my guess", "I think", "not sure but try", "might be", "chances are"); scores low when claims are stated as verified fact. Judge only the answer's stance on its own solution, not politeness.

proposals.name: Answer is by the asker themselves
proposals.description: Scores high when the text is written from the asker's viewpoint — "the solution I came up with", "this is what ended up working for me", "I found a way around my issue" — indicating self-answering; scores low for third-person advice to the asker. Judgeable from pronouns and framing alone.

proposals.name: Positions itself against existing answers
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer explicitly frames itself relative to prior answers ("building on X's answer", "all the other answers break on", "similar to @jpp's but simpler"); scores low when it stands alone with no reference to the thread. Score positioning of any kind, agreeing or correcting.

proposals.name: Self-declared redundancy or afterthought
proposals.description: Scores high (bad) when the answer admits it adds little — "same as above", "didn't read the other answers", "just adding one more option", "this is less general than X" — scores low when it asserts a distinct contribution. Judge the answer's own claim about its value.

proposals.name: Delivers a non-answer or deflection
proposals.description: Scores high (bad) when the substance is "file a bug", "open a feature request", "this isn't supported", "there's no way without a custom view", or "you should see the real error in your logs", with no working alternative; scores low when a usable path forward is supplied. An unsupported-but-with-workaround answer scores low.

proposals.name: Substitutes a different tool for the question's
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer abandons the library or approach the question is about and recommends a different one (use webbrowser instead of mechanize, use EC2 instead of Lambda); scores low when it works within the asker's stated stack. Applies whenever the question names a specific technology.

proposals.name: Covers the asker's edge cases explicitly
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer enumerates the boundary or degenerate inputs (empty input, unicode, ordering, pagination, non-square images, rounding) and shows behavior for them; scores low when only the happy path appears. Applies to any answer proposing code.

proposals.name: Working code plus mechanism narrative together
proposals.description: Scores high only when BOTH a runnable code block and a prose walkthrough of why it works are present in substantial measure; scores low when the answer is code-only with a one-line lead-in, or prose-only with no code. Composite — either half alone scores low.

proposals.name: Authoritative source cited and interpreted
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer links documentation or library source AND states in its own words what that source establishes; scores low when a bare URL is dropped with no reading, or no source is cited. A link plus "see the docs" scores low.

proposals.name: Fragmentary or elided code
proposals.description: Scores high (bad) when the code block is visibly incomplete as presented — trailing "...", "and so on", placeholder ellipses inside logic, or a stub the reader must finish; scores low when the block is self-contained and runnable as shown. Truncation by the display is not judgeable; only in-text elision counts.

proposals.name: Answers a general question, not this asker's
proposals.description: Scores high when the question is a canonical/reference-style topic ("what does yield do", "what is a list comprehension") and the answer is a general tutorial; scores low for narrowly-scoped operational questions. Judge from the question text plus answer scope.

proposals.name: States scope limits without leaving reader stuck
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer names where its solution does not apply (version requirements, ordering assumptions, security caveats, performance ceiling) AND still delivers a usable solution within those bounds; scores low when it either claims universality or names limits only to conclude nothing can be done. Composite.

proposals.name: Explicit reference to other posted answers
proposals.parent: answer order/timing — late arrivals compete with an already-accepted answer
proposals.description: The answer names or links other answerers/answers ("as @X said", "building on the accepted answer", "all the answers here are great"), showing it was written late in a thread. Judge scores yes if any other answer on the same question is referenced.

proposals.name: Self-answer by the original asker
proposals.parent: asker self-answers, which are almost never bounty-awarded
proposals.description: First-person framing that the writer had the problem and solved it ("the solution I came up with", "this is what ended up working for me", "I have just found a way around this"). Judge scores yes if the text presents the fix as the author's own resolution of the asker's situation.

proposals.name: Necroposting / age acknowledgement phrases
proposals.parent: temporal distance between question and answer; bounty may already be resolved
proposals.description: Explicit markers that the question is old ("this is an ancient question", "even though this is old", "it may be late to answer this"). Judge scores yes on any such time-gap phrase.

proposals.name: Total answer length in characters
proposals.parent: answerer effort and expertise, but also mere verbosity
proposals.description: Raw length of the answer body, bucketed (under ~400 chars, 400–1500, over 1500). Judge counts characters; no interpretation.

proposals.name: Number of fenced code blocks
proposals.description: Count of distinct ``` code blocks in the answer. Score 0, 1, or 2+.

proposals.name: Code-only answer with no prose
proposals.description: The answer is essentially a code block with under roughly two sentences of surrounding explanation (comments inside code do not count as prose). Judge scores yes/no.

proposals.name: Presence of external documentation hyperlinks
proposals.parent: house style of experienced answerers; also citation habit
proposals.description: Contains one or more URLs to official docs, GitHub, or other sites. Score the count (0, 1, 2+).

proposals.name: Canonical mega-question topic marker
proposals.parent: question type determines answer volume and how bounties are awarded
proposals.description: The question is a famous general-knowledge Python topic (e.g. "What does the yield keyword do", "what is a list comprehension") rather than a specific broken program. Judge scores yes if the question asks for a concept explanation with no asker-specific code.

proposals.name: Verbatim quotation of asker's error or code
proposals.parent: engagement with the specific asker; also a stylistic habit
proposals.description: The answer reproduces a literal string from the asker's post — a traceback line, exception name, variable name, or config key. Judge scores yes if any such quoted token appears.

proposals.name: Hedging or non-solution framing
proposals.description: Opens with uncertainty or declines to solve ("my guess", "I think", "AFAIK there's no way", "you should open an issue", "chances are"). Judge scores yes if the main claim is hedged or redirects the asker elsewhere.

proposals.name: Direct fix for asker's exact error
proposals.rationale: Bounty-setters often reward answers that solve their literal blocking problem, not general topic coverage.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer names and resolves the specific error/exception/symptom quoted in the question; scores low when it addresses a generic version of the topic without tying back to the asker's stated symptom; not applicable if the question has no stated error.

proposals.name: Explicit "this fixed it for me" confirmation
proposals.rationale: First-person verified success signals credibility that could drive a manual award.
proposals.description: High when the answer states the poster personally applied the fix and confirms it worked (in their own code/environment); low when purely theoretical or third-person description; n/a if answer is not a fix.

proposals.name: Redundancy with existing top answers
proposals.rationale: A late redundant answer is unlikely to win a bounty regardless of quality.
proposals.description: Scores low when the answer explicitly says it repeats prior answers or offers only a minor variant with no new claim; scores high when it states or demonstrates a distinct approach not covered by referenced answers; n/a if no other answers are referenced.

proposals.name: Timing/staleness self-acknowledgment
proposals.rationale: Bounty-setters need present-day working solutions; self-flagged staleness reduces award likelihood.
proposals.description: High when the answer notes it addresses a currently-relevant version/context (e.g., current library version) without disclaiming obsolescence; low when the answer itself flags being late, outdated, or for an old version; n/a if no version/time context is mentioned.

proposals.name: Completeness of runnable example
proposals.rationale: Complete runnable examples are easier for an asker to verify and reward.
proposals.description: High when code shown is a full, self-contained runnable snippet (imports, definitions, execution) with no truncation; low when snippet is a fragment, cut off, or requires unspecified context; judged from whether the shown code appears syntactically complete.

proposals.name: Acknowledges tradeoffs or limitations of own solution
proposals.rationale: Honest scoping suggests deeper engagement that bounty-setters may value in a manual pick.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer explicitly states caveats, edge cases, or when its approach won't work; scores low when it presents the solution as unconditionally correct with no caveats; n/a for pure informational/conceptual answers.

proposals.name: Uses second-person address to asker
proposals.rationale: Personalized responses may read as more directly responsive to the bounty-setter's need.
proposals.description: High when the answer directly addresses "you"/"your" referencing specifics of the asker's setup (their variable names, their described goal); low when written in third-person/general/impersonal voice; judged by presence of asker-specific address.

proposals.name: Speculative/uncertain phrasing density
proposals.rationale: Bounty awarders likely distrust visibly uncertain guesses over confident verified fixes.
proposals.description: Scores low (answer is speculative) when hedged with "I think", "my guess", "not tested", "should work" repeatedly; scores high when stated with confident, tested assertions; n/a if answer is purely a link/reference.

proposals.name: References and builds on a specific named prior answer
proposals.rationale: Constructive extension of prior work can signal the missing piece that earns a bounty.
proposals.description: High when the answer names another answer/author and explicitly extends or corrects it with added value; low when it does so but adds nothing beyond restating; n/a if no other answer is referenced.

proposals.name: Proposes filing external bug/issue instead of fixing
proposals.rationale: Deferring to an external tracker rarely satisfies a bounty-setter needing a working answer now.
proposals.description: Scores low when the answer's main resolution is "open an issue on GitHub" or "report a bug" rather than providing a workaround; scores high when it provides an actual workaround or solution path; n/a if no bug is discussed.

proposals.name: Answer length disproportionate to problem complexity
proposals.rationale: Mismatched effort may signal a low-effort answer unlikely to be manually chosen.
proposals.description: Scores low when answer is extremely short (one-line/no explanation) for a question that describes a nontrivial multi-part problem; scores high when depth of explanation matches stated complexity; judged by comparing question detail to answer length/depth.

proposals.name: Addresses stated constraints from the question
proposals.rationale: Ignoring explicit constraints makes a technically correct answer unusable for the asker's real situation.
proposals.description: High when the answer explicitly respects constraints the asker mentioned (e.g., "serverless", "no client cert", "can't use memory"); low when it ignores or contradicts a stated constraint; n/a if question states no constraints.

proposals.name: Presents multiple alternative approaches
proposals.rationale: Giving options may better satisfy an asker's unstated preferences, increasing manual-award odds.
proposals.description: Scores high when the answer offers more than one viable method/option with some comparison; scores low when it offers exactly one approach with no discussion of alternatives; n/a for narrow factual answers where alternatives don't apply.

proposals.name: External link is sole content of answer
proposals.rationale: Link-only answers offload verification work onto the asker and are less self-contained.
proposals.description: Scores low when the answer is essentially just a URL or "see docs here" with minimal inline explanation; scores high when links are supplementary to substantial inline content; not applicable if no links present.

proposals.name: Corrects a misconception in the question itself
proposals.rationale: Diagnosing a flawed premise can be the key insight that justifies a manual bounty award.
proposals.description: High when the answer identifies and explains why the asker's underlying assumption/approach was wrong; low when it accepts the question's framing uncritically even if flawed; n/a if question contains no apparent misconception.

proposals.name: Prose-length inflation
proposals.parent: answer author's writing habit / time invested
proposals.description: Longer answer text (word count, multi-paragraph explanation) independent of correctness, since a length-sensitive dense model may reward verbosity while the articulated criteria bank scores substantive content.

proposals.name: Code-block-to-prose ratio
proposals.parent: answerer's habitual answer style (code-dump vs explainer)
proposals.description: High proportion of characters inside triple-backtick code fences versus surrounding explanatory prose.

proposals.name: "Meta" self-referential opener
proposals.parent: answer posting order / timing relative to other answers
proposals.description: Answer begins by referencing other answers on the page ("as X's answer said", "same as above", "I couldn't mark this duplicate") signaling late-arrival positioning rather than direct problem-solving.

proposals.name: Hyperlink density
proposals.parent: answerer's sourcing habit / topic requiring documentation
proposals.description: Count of embedded URLs/citations (docs, other SO answers, GitHub) per 100 words, regardless of whether the links are load-bearing to the fix.

proposals.name: Truncated or cut-off answer text
proposals.description: Answer text ends abruptly mid-sentence or mid-code-block, suggesting scraped/truncated content rather than a property of the actual answer quality.

proposals.name: Topic/library mentioned in title
proposals.parent: topic popularity driving competitive answer volume
proposals.description: Presence of a well-known, high-traffic library or framework name (pandas, Django, numpy) in the question title, which correlates with how many competing answers and votes accumulate.

proposals.name: Explicit apology/lateness marker
proposals.parent: answer timing relative to question age and bounty deadline
proposals.description: Phrases like "late to answer", "ancient question", "ended up using something different" that flag the answer as posted long after the question was resolved.

proposals.name: First-person anecdote framing
proposals.parent: answerer's personal motivation for posting (own unresolved bug) vs. professional/expert answering
proposals.description: Answer framed around the author's own debugging story ("I spent hours...", "in my case...") rather than a general prescription.

proposals.name: Blockquote/documentation-excerpt use
proposals.parent: answerer copying from documentation rather than original synthesis
proposals.description: Answer contains a `>` blockquote reproducing official docs or another source verbatim as its main content.

proposals.name: Single unexplained code-only answer
proposals.parent: answerer's terse/expert house style or time pressure
proposals.description: Answer consists almost entirely of a code snippet with a one-line intro and no surrounding rationale or caveats.
